title: Data parallelism with Parallel and PLINQ
body: `Parallel.For` and `Parallel.ForEach` split CPU-bound loops across thread-pool threads; `Parallel.ForEachAsync` does the same for async bodies. They block until all iterations finish and aggregate exceptions into an `AggregateException`. `ParallelOptions` sets `MaxDegreeOfParallelism` and a cancellation token.

PLINQ adds `.AsParallel()` to a LINQ query to run operators on several threads. Results are unordered by default; `.AsOrdered()` preserves source order at some cost. `WithDegreeOfParallelism` and `WithCancellation` control execution. Side effects inside PLINQ lambdas are races unless protected.

Parallelism helps only when each item does enough CPU work to outweigh scheduling overhead and when the work is independent. Small loops, I/O-bound work and loops dominated by a shared lock often get slower. Measure with realistic data.

Use the thread-local overloads (`Parallel.For(from, to, localInit, body, localFinally)`) to accumulate per-thread results and combine them once, avoiding contention on a shared total. For floating-point sums, the combination order changes, so parallel results may differ in the last digits from a sequential sum.
Check iterations are independent, that shared results are combined safely, and that ordering requirements are explicit (`AsOrdered`, or sort afterwards).

challenge: Use PLINQ to find the five largest numbers below 100000 whose digit sum is 30, printing them in descending order.
question: By default, in what order does a PLINQ query produce results?
correct: Unspecified; use AsOrdered or sort to impose an order
reasoning: PLINQ partitions the input across threads; ordering costs extra and must be requested.
